newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - Brazil's Malan disputes cynics.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Brazil's Malan disputes cynics.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan, pouring cold water on market jitters over a ballooning trade deficit and slow progress on the fiscal front, said Brazil did not face any problems it could not resolve.
In an interview late Monday with Reuters, Malan said he was perfectly calm about the long-term prospects for Brazil's external accounts and the consolidated public sector deficit.

Displaying irritation with wariness among overseas investors and domestic "hysteria" over Brazil's worsening trade balance, he urged players to take a long-term view and to "probe deeper" behind the raw month-on-month macroeconomic figures.
"It's a short-term myopia, it's wrong to think the figures of one month can be projected over the next 12, the next 24 months," he said.

"You have to look at things over time, and with this long-term perspective in mind, the fiscal situation in Brazil will be better in 1996 than in 1995, better in 1997 than in 1996 and we are already working to make 1998 better than 1997."

Malan said the consolidated operational deficit was likely to be between 3.7-4.0 percent of gross domestic product this year, versus some 5.0 percent in 1995. "But what's important is the direction we're moving in," he said.

The U.S.-educated economist, who has overseen an economic stabilization plan that has brought hyperinflation down to what might be single digits this year, said a widening trade deficit this year was not a problem and the markets' fears were "wrong".

Brazilian Brady bonds and domestic markets have been nervous since Brazil posted a larger-than-expected trade deficit of $655 million in September and speculation has mounted October could be even worse, bringing the year-end deficit to some $4.0 billion against $3.157 billion in 1995.

But Malan said attention should be focused on the current account gap, which would be "less than 3.0 percent of GDP in 1996" and easily financed by record foreign direct investment and sovereign and corporate issues of high quality overseas.
Worries have also been growing in Brazil over the possibility of the government having to cool down an overheating economy next year in order to stem the tide of imports.
But Malan discarded this as a newspaper invention.

He said he foresaw "reasonable" GDP growth of 4.0-4.5 percent in 1997 after about 3.1 percent in 1996, and that there was no reason at all why the government would have to stimulate a contraction or an expansion of economic activity.
"Growth of 4.5 percent is not excessive," he said.

Malan said he was convinced exports would pick up, spurred by the recent exemption of some goods from so-called ICMS export tax, the revival of an export insurance agency and moves in the National Development Bank (BNDES) to alter export credit lines.

"Once again this takes time. Nothing happens overnight. We are convinced exports will respond," he said, adding that the government was continuing to take steps to boost overseas sales, such as the sell-off of ports, which would reduce costs.

The finance minister also brusquely dismissed fears Brazil would be unable next year to greatly reduce interest rates, among the highest in the world, because foreign capital would find the returns on Brazilian instruments unattractive.
He said the government had learned it could play around with the IOF tax, a tax on capital inflows and investments, in order to keep attracting foreign portfolio capital.

"We have always played around with the IOF if it seemed necessary to us," he said. Two weeks ago, the Brazilian government did exactly that, allowing banks to raise capital overseas and bring it into Brazil at a lower levy.
On the fiscal front, Malan said progress was being made in all areas of the consolidated public sector.
-- The states and cities were carrying out adjustment programs and selling off assets. He said their problem was "not debt, but cash flow".
-- Loss-making state-owned firms were being privatized.

-- The government had taken steps to eradicate social security distortions and intended to "reconstruct" its original social security reform in the Senate, where a vote was expected after the November 15 second round of municipal elections.
Malan said that if the picture looked worse just now, it was because some adjustments involved "up front costs", such as voluntary redundancy programs.
"It looks like an immediate deterioration, but it will clearly result in an improvement in the long-term," he said.
